messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 80
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Welder
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 54

She is 80 now, compact and strong through the shoulders from a lifetime of welding, with small burn scars on her forearms and a way of sitting that suggests she is always ready to brace. When she talks about her work, her face still brightens. She likes metal because it behaves according to heat, pressure, and patience. “Steel tells the truth,” she says. People, she has learned, do not always do that.

She meets her husband when she is young, long before she is a welder. At first he is charming in the ordinary ways that later become difficult to explain to other people. He brings her fruit, walks her home, tells her she is clever. He can also be jealous, though she does not name it that way then. He wants to know where she has been, who she has spoken to, why she took so long at the shop. After they marry, his temper becomes part of the architecture of the house. It arrives in slammed doors, accusations, long silences that force everyone else to move carefully around him.

The first time he hits her, she remembers the shock more than the pain. She is standing near the sink. He is angry about money, or supper, or some small thing that no longer seems worth separating from the rest. The blow feels unreal, almost administrative, as if a line has been crossed without warning and cannot be uncrossed. He apologizes afterward. He cries. He says he is ashamed, says it will never happen again. She believes him because she needs the world to remain something she can recognize.

But it happens again, and then many times. Over the years, the abuse becomes unpredictable enough that she is never fully at ease. Some nights she listens for the sound of his truck before it turns into the drive and feels her body tighten before her mind has caught up. She learns to read tiny changes in his face, the set of his jaw, the speed of his footsteps. She keeps rooms tidy, meals timed, her voice measured. She stops inviting people over. When relatives ask after her, she says he is under stress. She becomes skilled at arranging sleeves and makeup to hide bruises.

Work becomes the one place where she feels competent and solid. She trains as a welder in midlife, later than many of the men around her, and takes pride in doing a difficult job well. In the workshop, sparks fly and metal shrieks under the torch, but none of it frightens her. Noise there has a purpose. She likes the mask coming down over her face, the narrowed field of vision, the concentration. At work, she trusts her hands. At home, a cup dropped in the sink can make her heart race so hard she has to sit down. If a man raises his voice in the yard next door, she feels the old cold rush in her stomach and, for a moment, she is back in the kitchen, waiting.

Even after the physical violence lessens with age, she does not feel safe. His body is slower now, but his presence still governs the air in the house. She startles easily. When he enters a room unexpectedly, her shoulders jump and her breath catches before she can cover it. She sleeps lightly, waking at the smallest movement. Some nights she sees scenes from long ago with startling clarity: his hand closing around her wrist, the smell of beer, the pattern of linoleum beneath her cheek. She does not describe these as dreams at first. She says, “It comes back like it’s happening again.”

During the day, memories intrude while she is doing ordinary things. The flash from a welding arc can call up the flash of his belt buckle. The clang of metal can become the crack of something thrown against a wall. She loses time standing still, caught inside an image she does not want. She has spent decades trying not to think about what happened, packing it away in the same practical part of herself that got children fed and shifts covered and bills paid. But avoiding the memories has made her world smaller. She prefers staying in the shed or workshop to sitting in the house with him. She declines family gatherings if she thinks there may be drinking or loud arguments. Crowded places wear her out because she is always scanning, always locating exits, always noticing the men whose voices carry.

She feels shame for having stayed and another kind of shame for still being affected. At 80, she tells herself she should be beyond this. She has survived hard things, worked hard, raised a family, made a life. Yet her body does not care about those arguments. It reacts first and leaves her to explain afterward. Her husband, now old beside her, may ask an ordinary question and she hears danger in his tone before she can make sense of the words. Then she feels foolish, then angry, then tired.

What comes through most clearly is how long she has lived in a state of watchfulness. She describes never fully settling into a chair, never fully sleeping, never fully believing a peaceful day will remain peaceful. The trauma is not only in the memories of being hit. It is in the way she still organizes herself around the possibility of harm, as if some part of her remains in that earlier house, listening for footsteps, preparing to endure.
